# Opening Remarks {.headline-only}

## Make It Easy {.no-headline .vertical-center background-color="#0333ff"}

:::large
> Your job is to make it easy to say yes. *@thatcher2025rules*
:::

:::notes
@thatcher2025rules (Rule 15) observes that most papers are not rejected because they are wrong, but because they are hard to verify, hard to follow, or hard to trust. Editors and reviewers work under time pressure; a manuscript that anticipates their questions and makes verification effortless turns them into advocates.

This unit follows a manuscript through the publication process: submission, the editor's decision, the response to reviewers, and the communities in which the work circulates. It starts with the mock review the participants completed during the self-study phase.
:::

## Learning Outcomes

After completing this unit, you will be able to:

:::incremental
1. **Prepare** a complete submission, including authorship agreements and a cover letter.
2. **Interpret** editorial decisions and choose an adequate response.
3. **Respond** to reviewers with a structured response matrix and letter.
4. **Use** scholarly communities and doctoral consortia for feedback and visibility.
5. **Outline** a research agenda that connects your papers.
:::

# Mock Review Debrief {.headline-only}

## Decision Letter {.unlisted .unnumbered .html-hidden .discussion-slide}

:::medium
You are the editor
:::

Write the decision letter for the manuscript you edit, based on its two reviews:

1. State the **decision** (reject, major revision, minor revision, accept).
2. Synthesize the reviews into the **three to five issues** the revision has to address.
3. Indicate where the reviewers **disagree** and which position you support.

Use the [template](../admin/assets/APW_decision-letter-template.docx) and upload the letter to the Moodle folder *Decision Letter* by the end of the day.

{{< countdown "30:00" top="0">}}

:::notes
Writing a decision letter forces participants to do what editors do: weigh two reviews that often disagree, decide which concerns are essential, and translate them into a clear mandate for the revision. Keep the letter to about one page: a short summary of the manuscript and its potential, the decision, the numbered issues with a reference to the review comments they come from, and a closing sentence on what the revision has to achieve.
:::

## Decision Letters {.unlisted .unnumbered .html-hidden .discussion-slide}

:::medium
Feedback from the editor-in-chief
:::

For each manuscript (five minutes):

1. Is the **decision** covered by the two reviews?
2. Are the **priorities** of the revision clear?
3. How did the editor handle **disagreement** between the reviewers?

The editor of the manuscript reads the letter aloud; the lecturer comments as editor-in-chief.

{{< countdown "25:00" top="0">}}

:::notes
The debrief makes the editor's perspective explicit, which helps authors read their own decision letters: the letter, not the individual reviews, defines what the revision has to achieve. The authors hear their decision letter for the first time in the debrief and use it directly in the response matrix.
:::

# Submission {.headline-only}

## Authorship

:::incremental
- Agree on **who is an author** and the **order** before writing the final draft.
- All authors carry **full responsibility** for the content.
- Ask about the **policies** of your supervisor and your research group.
- Document **contributions,** e.g., with the CRediT roles [@brand2015beyond].
:::

:::notes
Authorship conflicts are among the most common problems in collaborative research, and they are easiest to avoid when the agreement comes early. The author team can be extended at a later stage, but before submission, and only if all authors agree and the order is aligned. Many journals now ask for a contributor statement; the CRediT taxonomy describes 14 roles (e.g., conceptualization, methodology, formal analysis, writing of the original draft, review and editing) that make individual contributions transparent [@brand2015beyond].

For cumulative dissertations, check the regulations of your doctoral program: they often require a statement on your own contribution to each co-authored paper and may limit the number of co-authors or the required author position.
:::

## Submission Checklist

:::smaller
:::incremental
- Text, tables, and figures are **numbered** consecutively; each table and figure is **referenced** in the text.
- Every table and figure is **understandable** without the text.
- Every in-text **citation** appears in the reference list, and vice versa; every reference is accurate.
- The manuscript meets the **requirements** of the journal (length, format, anonymization, abstract).
- **Statements** are ready: data availability, ethics approval, conflicts of interest, use of AI tools.
- Author **data** for all co-authors are at hand (affiliations, contact details, biographies).
- The final version has been **read twice,** the second time on a different day.
:::
:::

:::notes
The checklist combines the formal checks from the previous course with the transparency templates in @thatcher2025rules [Appendix H], which address sensitive data and non-standard design choices. Thatcher reports rejecting a paper because several sources were miscited: if the citations cannot be trusted, reviewers stop trusting the empirics as well [@thatcher2025rules, Rule 12].

After submission, save the confirmation, inform your co-authors, and send them all submitted files, including the editable versions (e.g., Word and Excel files) if you submitted PDFs.
:::

## Cover Letter

:::smaller
> Dear Professor [Name],
>
> Please find enclosed our manuscript "[Title]," which we submit for consideration as a research article in [Journal].
>
> The manuscript examines [research question] in [context]. Drawing on [theory] and [data and method], we show that [core finding]. The study contributes to the conversation on [conversation] in [Journal], in particular to recent work by [authors published in the journal], by [contribution].
>
> The manuscript has not been published and is not under consideration elsewhere. All authors have approved the submission. [Required statements, e.g., on related conference papers or the use of AI tools.]
>
> Sincerely,
> [Corresponding author]
:::

:::notes
A cover letter does not replace the abstract; it tells the editor in a few sentences why the manuscript belongs in this journal. The strongest argument is the conversation: naming the journal's own recent contributions to the topic shows the editor that the paper continues a discussion the journal already hosts. Include all statements the journal requires, and disclose related publications such as an earlier conference version. Some journals ask for suggested or excluded reviewers; suggest scholars from the conversation without conflicts of interest.
:::

# Decisions {.headline-only}

## Decision Types

:::smaller
| Decision | Meaning | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| Desk reject | Not sent out for review (fit, contribution, quality) | Revise positioning, choose another outlet |
| Reject | Reviewed, not acceptable | Use the reviews, revise, submit elsewhere |
| Reject and resubmit | Not acceptable in its current form, new submission invited | Substantial rework, treated as a new submission |
| Major revision | Promising, substantial changes required | Revise and respond point by point |
| Minor revision | Close to acceptance | Revise and respond point by point |
| Accept | Accepted, possibly with conditions | Proofs, final files |

: Typical editorial decisions {#tbl-decisions}
:::

:::notes
The labels differ between journals; read the letter for what the editor asks, not only for the label. A major revision at a selective journal is an invitation to continue, not a verdict, and the effort of a careful revision is usually worth it. Withdrawing after a major revision makes sense only if the requested changes would turn the paper into a different paper that the authors do not want to write.

After an acceptance without revision, nothing remains to do until the proofs arrive, apart from a short note to thank the editor. After a minor revision, consider each suggestion and make the changes that improve the paper; explain in the response why you did not follow a recommendation.
:::

## Handling Rejection

:::incremental
- Take **time** before reacting: at least one night's sleep.
- **Use** the reviews: address the comments before submitting elsewhere.
- Expect **overlap:** the next journal may send the paper to the same reviewer.
- **Contest** a decision only if the judgment was clearly superficial or wrong, and only with a brief, polite letter.
:::

:::notes
Rejection is the most frequent outcome in academic publishing and is part of every career. The reviews of a rejected paper are free expert feedback; ignoring them risks meeting the same reviewer again with the same objections, which happens more often than authors expect in small fields. Appeals rarely succeed and should be reserved for clear errors, such as a review that addresses a different paper or rests on a factual misunderstanding.
:::

## Behind the Scenes {.html-hidden .unlisted}

:::medium
The history of one paper: from first draft to publication
:::

:::notes
The lecturer shows the history of one of their own papers: the submitted version, the reviews and the decision letter, the response letter, and the published version. Questions for the group: Which reviewer comments changed the paper most? Which ones did the authors reject, and how did they argue? How long did the process take, and where did the time go?
:::

# Responding {.headline-only}

## Response Letter

:::incremental
- **Thank** the editor and the reviewers; keep the tone factual throughout.
- Respond to **every** point; quote each comment verbatim.
- State **what** you changed and **where** (page, section, table).
- **Disagree** with evidence and offer an alternative fix.
- Start with the editor's **priorities.**
:::

:::notes
The response letter is the document the editor and the reviewers read first in the next round; it determines whether they read the revised manuscript as an improvement. Quoting each comment verbatim and answering directly beneath it lets reviewers verify the changes without searching. When you disagree, explain why, refer to evidence or literature, and offer a different way to address the underlying concern (e.g., a boundary condition, an additional analysis, a clarifying footnote) [@thatcher2025rules, Appendix G]. Reviewers accept a well-argued disagreement more readily than an evasive change.
:::

## Response Matrix

:::smaller
| Issue (verbatim) | Evidence | Fix | Rule invoked | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1.3: "The definition of X overlaps with Y." | p. 7, section 2.2 | Added contrastive definition and table of neighboring constructs | One construct, one paragraph | Accepted |
| R2.1: "Collect additional longitudinal data." | p. 21, limitations | Stated temporal boundary condition; added robustness check with lagged data | Theorize, don't speculate | Rejected (rationale and alternative) |

: Response-to-reviewers matrix, adapted from @thatcher2025rules [Appendix G] {#tbl-response-matrix}
:::

:::notes
@thatcher2025rules proposes a one-page matrix that turns a revise-and-resubmit into a project plan. Each row contains one discrete issue, quoted verbatim, the location where the issue is visible, the change made, the rule or principle the change applies, and the result (accepted, or rejected with a brief rationale). Number and cluster the issues (e.g., theory, methods, results) so that the editor can scan them, and keep a version date and the review round in the header. The matrix serves as the internal plan; the response letter is written from it.
:::

Response matrix

# Community {.headline-only}

## Scholarly Communities

:::incremental
- **Associations and subgroups:** divisions of the Academy of Management, special interest groups of the AIS, scientific commissions of the VHB
- **Doctoral consortia** at major conferences (e.g., ICIS, ECIS, Academy of Management)
- **PhD seminars,** e.g., the AIS SIG DITE PhD Research Seminar
- **Reviewing** for conferences as an entry point into a community
:::

:::notes
The conversations that the first day mapped are carried by communities. Associations organize them in subgroups (divisions, special interest groups, scientific commissions), which run conference tracks, workshops, awards, and doctoral programs. Joining the subgroup that hosts your conversation gives access to the people who will later review your work.

Doctoral consortia bring a small group of doctoral candidates together with senior scholars for feedback on their dissertation projects; admission is competitive and usually requires a short proposal. PhD seminars such as the AIS SIG DITE PhD Research Seminar on digital innovation, transformation, and entrepreneurship run over several weeks, combine readings with discussions led by leading scholars, and end with a paper development workshop. Reviewing for conferences is the easiest way in: it trains the reviewer's perspective, and track chairs remember reliable reviewers.
:::

## Research Agenda

:::medium
A research agenda is a long-term, strategic roadmap of **interrelated studies** that builds a scholarly identity [@thatcher2025agenda].
:::

:::incremental
- It **focuses** attention on a problem and defines the audience for your work.
- It helps to decide whether to take on a new paper or learn a new method.
- Research is **messy:** stay problem-centric and accept that some papers lay foundations.
:::

:::notes
@thatcher2025agenda recommends developing a research agenda through the systematic scaffolding of theoretical ideas, the purposeful development of methodological skills, and the explicit incorporation of practical impact. He also stresses that research is rarely linear: it is messy, non-linear, and sometimes opportunistic. The way to add structure to such a process is to stay focused on one problem and to accept that some papers serve as foundations for others.
:::

## Paper Sets

:::incremental
- A **coherent series** of related papers around a core problem
- Each paper deepens **theoretical, empirical, or practical** understanding.
- Not all papers appear in top journals; **foundational papers** (review, method tutorial, practice paper) prepare the core contribution.
- The papers are **synergistic** and build your identity as a scholar [@thatcher2025agenda].
:::

:::notes
@thatcher2025agenda illustrates paper sets with his work on IT mindfulness: a tutorial and a measurement paper in other outlets built the conceptual and methodological foundation for a construct and theory paper in MIS Quarterly and a field experiment in the Journal of Management Information Systems. The foundational papers showed technical skill, built trust with the community, and framed the conversation.

For cumulative dissertations, the paper set and the dissertation coincide: the framing paper explains how the individual papers address one core problem and how together they make a contribution that exceeds the sum of the parts.
:::

# Wrap-Up {.headline-only}

## Pre-Submission Board {.unlisted .unnumbered .html-hidden .discussion-slide}

:::medium
One slide, three minutes
:::

Present your manuscript on **one slide:** title, model or central argument, and a one-sentence contribution.

The group gives a **submission recommendation:**

- **Submit** to the target outlet now
- **Revise first** (name the one thing that has to change)
- **Reposition** (name a better-fitting outlet or conversation)

{{< countdown "25:00" top="0">}}

:::notes
The format applies the teachability test from @thatcher2025rules (Rule 17): a manuscript whose argument can be explained on one slide in three minutes has a clear structure. Compare the contribution sentence with the elevator pitch from the first day; the difference shows how the manuscript has developed during the course.
:::

## Publication Plan {.unlisted .unnumbered .html-hidden .discussion-slide}

:::medium
Your next steps
:::

1. **Manuscript:** target outlet and planned submission date
2. **Next three steps,** each with a date
3. **Community:** one association, subgroup, consortium, or seminar you will engage with
4. **Paper set:** how this manuscript relates to your other papers
